def: Combining the weights of several models, usually fine-tunes of one base, into a single model by arithmetic on the weights and without gradient training.
The average of the weights of several models fine-tuned from the same pre-trained model, which often beats the best single member at no extra inference cost.
The difference between a fine-tuned model's weights and the weights of the base it started from, describing everything that fine-tuning changed.
Adding or subtracting scaled task vectors from a base model to add, combine or remove behaviours.
Spherical linear interpolation: blending two weight tensors along the arc between them so that their norm is not shrunk in the middle.
Loss of ability when task vectors are combined because many entries are redundant noise or because different models push the same weight in opposite directions.
A merge method that trims small task-vector entries, elects a sign for each weight and averages only the entries that agree with it.
A merge pre-processing step that randomly drops a fraction p of a task vector's entries and rescales the rest by 1/(1-p), keeping the expected update unchanged.
The configuration of a merge: which models, which method, and the weights and densities per model or per layer, kept as a versioned file.
Searching for a merge recipe with an evolutionary algorithm that merges and scores candidate recipes, in parameter space and in data-flow space, without gradients.

term: Search set versus held-out test set
def: The data an optimiser is allowed to score candidates on, kept separate from the data used once at the end to report the final result, because search overfits its own score.
